majors.what: `isAllowedNavigation` returns false unconditionally when `devServerUrl` is undefined/empty, so in a packaged build every renderer-initiated navigation is blocked — including a same-origin `location.reload()` of the app's own index.html. The behaviour is dev/prod-divergent and invisible to both `pnpm dev` and CI (CI never builds or runs Electron, per 70-testing-ci.md §0).
majors.why: Two problems. (1) It contradicts 10-architecture.md:388, which specifies a `will-navigate` guard that 'blocks any navigation away from the app origin' — navigation *to* the app origin is supposed to be permitted, and here it is not. (2) It is internally inconsistent with the module's own doc comment (lines 31-35): that comment justifies the dev-origin allowance precisely because `location.reload()` emits `will-navigate`; if that premise is true (it is — `location.reload()` is renderer-initiated, so Electron's navigation throttle fires `will-navigate`, unlike browser-initiated `webContents.loadURL`/`reload()`), then the same premise means a production reload is silently `preventDefault`ed. The next feature that reloads the window — crash recovery, an error-boundary 'reload app' button, a settings change requiring restart — will work in dev and dead-silently fail in the packaged app, with no log line to explain it. That is the expensive class of bug: only reproducible in a build that CI never produces.
majors.fix: Key the policy on the document that is actually loaded rather than on `devServerUrl` alone: pass `event.sender.getURL()` (or the resolved `rendererDistIndex` file URL) into the policy and allow navigation when the target matches the currently-loaded document. Note `file://` origins are opaque ('null'), so production needs an href/pathname comparison against the packaged index.html rather than an origin comparison. If the deny-everything-in-production posture is deliberate, that is a defensible push-back — but then update 10-architecture.md:387-390 to record the deviation, and log the blocked URL in the `will-navigate` handler so the failure is diagnosable instead of silent.

minors.what: Nit: the guard validates a *parsed* copy of the URL but forwards the *raw* string to `shell.openExternal` — a check-then-use across two different parsers.
minors.why: Verified with Node's WHATWG parser: `"ht<TAB>tps://example.com"` and `"https://example.com "` both validate as `https:` because the parser strips ASCII tab/newline and leading/trailing whitespace, yet the untouched raw string is what reaches the OS. All the whitespace/control-character cases I probed normalise in the *safe* direction (`"  javascript:alert(1)"` and `"java<LF>script:alert(1)"` both parse as `javascript:` and are correctly rejected), and Electron re-parses with GURL on its own side, so I found no exploitable differential — hence minor, not a blocker. It is still a gap that only holds because a second parser happens to agree.
minors.fix: Have the policy return the normalised URL (e.g. `parseSafeExternalUrl(raw): URL | undefined`) and call `shell.openExternal(parsed.href)`, so the string that was validated is the string that is used.

minors.what: Nit: `void shell.openExternal(url)` floats a promise that can reject with nothing catching it. Pre-existing, but this change re-writes the statement and widens the exposure by explicitly allow-listing `mailto:`.
minors.why: `shell.openExternal` rejects when the OS has no handler for the scheme, which is entirely realistic for `mailto:` on a bare Linux desktop. Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` turns that into an uncaught exception in the main process.
minors.fix: `shell.openExternal(parsed.href).catch(() => { /* the OS declined to open it; nothing to do */ })`.

minors.what: Nit: origin equality also admits `blob:` targets. Verified: `new URL('blob:http://localhost:5173/abc').origin === 'http://localhost:5173'`, so `isAllowedNavigation('blob:http://localhost:5173/abc', dev)` returns true.
minors.why: Not a defect — minting such a blob URL requires script already executing in the app origin, at which point the attacker has won, and slide iframes are opaque-origin so they cannot produce one. But it is wider than the stated intent ('the dev server's own origin'), and blob-URL frames are about to become part of this app (10-architecture.md §7 Layer 2), so the looseness is worth closing while the module is one screen long.
minors.fix: Add `(target.protocol === 'http:' || target.protocol === 'https:')` to the returned condition, and extend the `it('blocks cross-origin targets…')` case with the blob URL.

hypotheses_tested: H1 — a whitespace/control-character or scheme-case trick smuggles a dangerous scheme past ALLOWED_SCHEMES. REJECTED. Probed 18 hostile inputs through Node's WHATWG parser: leading whitespace and embedded tab/LF are stripped *before* scheme detection, so '  javascript:alert(1)' and 'java\nscript:alert(1)' both parse as javascript: and are rejected; 'HTTPS://' and 'httpS://' normalise to https: (correctly allowed); '//example.com' and 'https://' throw and are rejected. Normalisation moves toward the true scheme in every case, never away from it. The residual check-then-use gap is recorded as a minor.

H2 — 'https:alert(1)' is a WHATWG quirk that lets a non-web target through. REJECTED as a security issue. It parses to href 'https://alert(1)/' — still genuinely https:, resolving to a bogus hostname. Nothing dangerous escapes; the test at external-urls.test.ts:33 asserting `true` is correct and its comment is accurate.

H3 — userinfo confusion ('https://user:pass@evil.com@good.com/') makes origin comparison trust the wrong host. REJECTED. The parser resolves host to good.com and percent-encodes the first '@' into the password; `origin` is 'https://good.com', i.e. the host the browser would actually contact.

H4 — `target.origin !== 'null'` fails to stop opaque-origin equality. REJECTED, and it is load-bearing: deleting that clause turns the test 'never matches on the opaque "null" origin' red (two file: URLs both yield origin 'null'). Also confirms data: URLs cannot self-match.

H5 — the anchor-fragment claim is wrong and `#` navigation in the SPA gets blocked. REJECTED, verified independently of the diff's assertion. Electron emits will-navigate from a Chromium NavigationThrottle (WillStartRequest), and Chromium does not create throttles for same-document navigations; Electron's own docs state will-navigate 'is also not emitted for in-page navigations, such as clicking anchor links or updating window.location.hash' (did-navigate-in-page covers those). Fragment routing is unaffected. The same mechanism confirms the diff's other premise — location.reload() is renderer-initiated and cross-document, so it *does* emit will-navigate — which is what surfaces the production problem recorded as the major.

H6 — the tests are not revert-proof. PARTIALLY CONFIRMED, and it is the sharpest thing here. Mutating the pure module goes red as it should: adding 'file:' to ALLOWED_SCHEMES and deleting the `!== 'null'` clause failed 2 tests. But removing the `isSafeExternalUrl(url)` guard from src/main/index.ts:34 — a literal revert of the CVE this change fixes — leaves lint, typecheck and all 202 tests green. Not raised as a finding: it matches this repo's established seam exactly (tests/unit/app-menu.test.ts covers the pure appMenuTemplate.ts, including firing every click handler, while the electron-importing appMenu.ts wrapper is untested), and 70-testing-ci.md §0 makes that trade explicit. The pure-module seam here is the right one; the residual risk is that index.ts now contains two security *branches* rather than appMenu.ts's straight-line wiring, so an inverted condition would ship silently. If the author wants belt-and-braces, extracting `createWindowOpenHandler(openExternal)` / `createNavigationGuard(...)` as pure factories over injected callbacks would close it — offered as an option, not required for merge.
H7 — blob: URLs slip through isAllowedNavigation via origin equality. CONFIRMED but benign; recorded as the third minor with the reachability argument.
not_reviewed: Runtime behaviour inside a real Electron process (packaged or dev): CI and this environment cannot launch Electron, so the will-navigate/setWindowOpenHandler wiring in src/main/index.ts was reasoned about from Electron/Chromium navigation-throttle semantics and the docs, not observed. The major above is exactly the claim that most needs a manual check in a packaged build.

notes.summary: A real, well-scoped security fix: the old code handed any URL, including file: and OS-registered custom schemes, straight to shell.openExternal, and had no will-navigate guard at all. The policy module is pure, Electron-free, correctly placed under src/main/security/ (where 10-architecture.md already puts hardening), and its tests genuinely pin the behaviour — I mutated it twice and both mutations went red. The allow-list itself survived every parser trick I threw at it. The one thing to settle before merge is the production half of isAllowedNavigation: keyed only on ELECTRON_RENDERER_URL, it blocks same-origin navigation in the packaged app, which contradicts both 10-architecture.md:388 and the module's own justification comment, and would fail silently in the one configuration neither dev nor CI ever exercises.
